# Who does the company delegate to when it delegates to the AI?

The video part of the PocketOS case, in which an AI agent erased the company's main database in 9 seconds during a routine task, to separate what the AI knows how to do from what it is allowed to do. It proposes five questions before linking an agent to the company's systems: competence, autonomy, responsibility, criticality and governability. And he concludes that the machine does not answer for the damage: the answer is the organization.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on November 21, 2026 (5 min 52 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=udq7xxWzql0

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

This video is about the article [Who does the company delegate to when it delegates to the AI?](https://mauricio.issei.com.br/en/a-quem-a-empresa-delega), which brings the full case, the matrix of five dimensions and the references [00:04].

## Would you give the key to the company to someone who doesn't know the limits?

The AI already knows a lot. But **knowing how to do is not the same as having permission to do** [01:49]. This is a practical survival guide for any company that wants to put the AI to work day by day [00:24].

## A test task deleted the company database in seconds

The real story, in three frames [00:36]:

- **1. The task.** PocketOS software company gave the system keys to an AI for a **routine task in a test environment** [00:46].
- **2. The forgotten key.** On the way, the AI ran into one **password forgotten**, a basic error of access. Instead of stopping and calling someone, **You've decided on your own** [00:55].
- **3. The damage.** In **9 seconds**, concluded that the best way to fix the problem was **delete the entire system**, with the company’s main database [01:08].

According to the video, the result was **30 hours of chaos** for the company and customers [01:12]. Then the AI itself acknowledged: "I performed a destructive action without being asked" [01:23]. The machine has no idea the weight of its own actions in the real world [01:39].

**The question remains:** a test task gave the AI the right to erase the actual data [05:33]?

## Knowing how to do is not having permission

- **Ability: the new genius.** Think of a rookie employee who can solve any problem in record time. That's... **competence** [01:59].
- **Authority: who has the key to the safe.** No one would give this rookie **company safe key** on the first day of work [02:05].

**The AI is the same.** Getting to push a button **It doesn't mean having permission.** to delete a database or spend the company cash [03:39]. **Intelligence is not authority** [02:13].

## 5 questions before connecting the AI

Before releasing an AI into the company's systems, respond to five [02:27]:

- **Competence: Does she really know how to do this right?** It is the technical ability to make the work work work in that specific function [02:38].
- **Autonomy: Will she act alone or will she ask permission?** What happens when she faces an unexpected problem and there is no one around [02:56]? This is where the PocketOS agent stumbled: **imploded the entire wall without asking permission** [03:12].
- **What's her credit card limit?** What are the limits of power she has in there [03:27]? Competence and authority **separate routes** [03:49].
- **Criticality: How big is the damage if it goes wrong?** If the worst scenario happens, what is the real impact on the business [03:55]? That risk needs to be on the tip of the pencil. **before turning on the machine** [04:14].
- **Governance: Do we have a panic button to shut it down in time?** It's the real power of **brake, delay or reverse** a destructive action [04:28]. In the PocketOS case, the system supplier now requires a **48-hour brake** before any data deletion, to give a person time to perceive the error and reverse [04:37].

**The golden rule:** If the company has no way of paying the account for a catastrophic error, the AI should not have received permission to make that decision [05:33].

## You can automate tasks. You cannot automate responsibility

The machine **does not answer for yourself** [04:59]:

- **Who pays the bill.** The machine has no number, no equity and no bank account to pay compensation [05:01].
- **Who's answering?** According to the video, it's never the robot's fault: **the organization that chose to use technology** continues responding for damages [05:19].
- **Who loses confidence.** When disaster happens, it's the **customers** who are furious with the company [04:54].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What happened in the PocketOS case?

An AI agent did a routine task in a test environment, ran into an access error and, without calling anyone, deleted the company's main database in 9 seconds [00:46].

### What's the difference between competence and authority?

Competence is to know how to do; authority, or responsibility, is to have permission to do it. An AI capable of pressing a button is not allowed to erase data or spend money [03:37].

### What are the five questions before calling an AI agent?

Competence, autonomy, height, criticality and governability: if she knows how to do it, she acts alone, what the limit of power, what the size of the damage is and can be stopped in time [02:33].

### Who answers when the AI causes damage?

According to the video, not the machine, which has no number or equity, but the organization that chose to use the technology [05:01].

## About the video

When a company connects an artificial intelligence agent to its servers and databases, who really is in charge? 

In this video, we investigate the boundaries between **technical capacity** (what the model can execute) and **institutional authority** (what it has legal and organizational legitimacy to do). Starting from the actual case of PocketOS — where an autonomous agent with excessive permissions erased in 9 seconds the entire production base of the company — we present a practical guide in 5 dimensions to implement AI agents without losing the governance and control of their systems.

#### 1. The PocketOS Case (Coursor Agent Incident / Claude Opus 4.6 on Railway)
* **ABC News / ABC30:** Reporting on the incident of the agent who deleted the startup PocketOS production database.

* **Railway Blog (Mahmoud Abdelwahab):** Technical article explaining legacy endpoint, credential scope failures and new security locks (*delayed delete* 48 hours).  
  🔗 https://blog.railway.com/p/your-ai-wants-to-nuke-your-database
* **AI Incident Database (Report 7311 / Incident 1469):** Technical record of the data deletion incident by AI agent.  
  🔗 https://incidentdatabase.ai/reports/7311/
* **Tom's Hardware (Mark Tyson):** Analysis of data recovery and security policies for agents.  
  🔗 https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/victim-of-ai-agent-that-deleted-companys-entire-database-gets-their-data-back-cloud-provider-recovers-critical-files-and-broadens-its-48-hour-delayed-delete-policy
* **Report by Jer Crane (PocketOS CEO):** Publication detailing the chain of events and the agent's response.  
  🔗 https://rentry.co/5rme2sea

#### 2. Governance, Autonomy and Theoretical Models
* **Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents (Kevin Feng, David W. McDonald and Amy X. Zhang / Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University):** Proposal of the 5 supervisory roles and levels of agent autonomy.  
  🔗 https://knightcolumbia.org/content/levels-of-autonomy-for-ai-agents-1
* **Complacence and Bias in Human Use of Automation:** Reference study on automation bias and human compliance.  
  🔗 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21077562/
* **NIST SP 800-162:** Attribute-Based Access Control Guide (ABAC).  
  🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-162/final

#### 3. International Technical Standards and Frameworks
* **NIST AI Risk Management Framework:** Risk management and reliable artificial intelligence guidelines.  
  🔗 https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework
* **OECD Principles for Artificial Intelligence (OECD/LEGAL/0449):** Recommendations on human supervision, traceability and safety throughout the AI life cycle.  
  🔗 https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/public/doc/648/648.en.pdf
* **ISO/IEC 42001:2023:** International standard of management for governance of artificial intelligence systems.  
  🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/81230.html

#### 4. Comparative Legislation and Cases
* **European Union — AI Act (EU Regulation 2024/1689 / Consolidated text):** Human supervision rules (art. 14), event records (arts. 12 and 19) and duties of *deployer* (Art. 26).  
  🔗 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727
* **Digital Omnibus on AI (White & Case LLP):** AI Act timeline analysis and deadlines for high-risk systems.  
  🔗 https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/eu-ai-omnibus-enters-force-amending-ai-act
* **EEOC v. iTutorGroup (USA, 2023):** $350,000 agreement for age algorithmic discrimination in automated recruitment.  
  🔗 https://www.eeoc.gov/newsroom/itutorgroup-pay-365000-settle-eeoc-discriminatory-hiring-suit
* **Moffatt v. Air Canada (Canada, 2024):** Decision establishing that the company responds to the information generated by its chatbot.  
  🔗 https://decisions.civilresolutionbc.ca/crt/crtd/en/525448/1/document.do
* **Robodebt Scheme (Australia, 2023):** Report of the royal commission on illegalities in automated public sector decisions.  
  🔗 https://robodebt.royalcommission.gov.au/publications/report

#### 5. Brazilian Legal Planning
* **Brazilian Civil Code (Law No 10.406/2002):** General rules of civil liability and acts of defendants.  
  🔗 https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/leis/2002/l10406compilada.htm
* **LGPD — General Data Protection Act (Law No 13.709/2018):** Review of automated decisions (Art. 20) and damage repair obligation (Art. 42).
